The controlled biological decomposition of organic wastes (food scraps, yard waste) by aerobic microbes into nutrient-rich soil humus
Burying plastic electronics and car tyres in garden beds
10.explanation: Aerobic thermophilic bacteria and fungi break down cellulose and lignin into dark organic compost, restoring soil structure and fertility.

10.question: What is 'e-waste' (electronic waste)?
options: Electricity bills sent to consumers by postal mail
Discarded electrical or electronic equipment (computers, mobile phones, televisions, refrigerators) containing hazardous heavy metals and plastics
Old printed books and magazines stored in school libraries
Broken wooden tables and chairs discarded by offices
10.explanation: E-waste represents the fastest-growing solid waste stream globally, containing both valuable gold/copper and neurotoxic lead/cadmium.

10.question: Why does informal e-waste recycling (e.g. at Agbogbloshie in Ghana) cause severe environmental and health hazards?
options: It causes all city water pipes to freeze into solid ice blocks
It makes workers grow wings and fly through the air
It turns broken mobile phones into pure gold bars without any heat
Open-air wire burning and acid leaching release carcinogenic dioxins, lead, and mercury into local soils, air, and waterways, poisoning workers
10.explanation: Manual smelting and primitive cyanide baths expose impoverished child workers and estuarine ecosystems to lethal bioaccumulative heavy metals.

10.question: Which international treaty regulates and restricts the transboundary movement and disposal of hazardous wastes (including e-waste)?
options: The Ramsar Convention
The Montreal Protocol
The Basel Convention
The Kyoto Protocol
10.explanation: The Basel Convention mandates prior informed consent (PIC) and bans developed nations from dumping toxic wastes into developing countries.

10.question: What are the 'United Nations Sustainable Development Goals' (SDGs)?
options: Seventeen rules for building commercial skyscrapers in cities
A military alliance formed by seventeen northern nations
A list of seventeen sports played in the Olympic Games
A universal set of 17 interconnected global goals adopted in 2015 to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure prosperity for all by 2030
10.explanation: The 2030 Agenda establishes 17 goals and 169 targets bridging climate action, poverty eradication, clean energy, and life below water.

10.question: Which UN Sustainable Development Goal specifically targets 'Affordable and Clean Energy'?
options: SDG 7
SDG 3
SDG 14
SDG 1
10.explanation: SDG 7 aims to ensure universal access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy services for all by 2030.

10.question: Which UN Sustainable Development Goal specifically targets 'Climate Action'?
options: SDG 13
SDG 8
SDG 2
SDG 10
10.explanation: SDG 13 urges immediate concerted international action to combat climate change and mitigate its devastating socioeconomic impacts.

10.question: Which UN Sustainable Development Goal focuses on 'Life Below Water'?
options: SDG 14
SDG 5
SDG 11
SDG 16
10.explanation: SDG 14 addresses marine conservation, overfishing, marine pollution, acidification, and the sustainable exploitation of ocean resources.

10.question: Which UN Sustainable Development Goal focuses on 'Life on Land'?
options: SDG 15
SDG 6
SDG 4
SDG 12
10.explanation: SDG 15 focuses on protecting terrestrial ecosystems, sustainable forestry, combating desertification, and halting biodiversity loss.

10.question: What is 'Life Cycle Assessment' (LCA) of a product?
options: Measuring the physical weight of a product using laboratory scales
A comprehensive methodology evaluating the environmental impacts of a product across its entire life cycle: from raw material extraction to disposal ('cradle to grave')
Calculating the retail sales profit of a product in supermarkets
A medical examination given to factory workers once every five years
10.explanation: LCA quantifies inputs (energy, water, materials) and outputs (emissions, solid waste) from raw extraction through manufacturing to disposal.

10.question: What does a 'Cradle-to-Cradle' (C2C) design philosophy advocate?
options: Manufacturing products intended to break and be thrown away in one week
Designing products so that all materials can be perpetually disassembled and recycled into technical or biological nutrients with zero waste
Burying baby cots in municipal landfill dumps after use
Using toxic chemicals to make products last longer without recycling
10.explanation: C2C eliminates the concept of waste entirely, creating closed regenerative loops where technical polymers and biological nutrients circulate safely.

10.question: What is 'planned obsolescence' in industrial manufacturing?
options: Designing products with an artificially limited useful life so they break, wear out, or become obsolete quickly, forcing repeat consumer purchases
Recycling 100% of all factory waste back into clean raw materials
Testing products rigorously to ensure they last for over a hundred years
Offering free lifetime replacement parts for broken household appliances
10.explanation: Planned obsolescence artificially drives linear consumer throughput, generating massive volumes of premature e-waste and material exhaustion.

10.question: What does the 'Right to Repair' consumer movement advocate?
options: A law ordering all citizens to become certified automobile mechanics
Legislation requiring manufacturers to provide fair access to replacement parts, repair manuals, and software tools so consumers can repair their devices
A ban on using tools or screwdrivers in residential homes
A government tax charged every time an appliance breaks down
10.explanation: Right to Repair curbs monopolistic electronic design, extending product lifespans and dramatically reducing unnecessary e-waste generation.

10.question: What is 'greenwashing' by corporations?
options: Washing the windows of corporate office buildings with clean water
Misleading consumers by marketing a company's products or policies as environmentally friendly when they are actually environmentally destructive
Planting real trees around corporate headquarters buildings
Painting company delivery trucks with bright green paint
10.explanation: Deceptive green PR masks continued fossil investments and environmental degradation behind superficial, unverified eco-marketing slogans.

10.question: What is an 'eco-label' on commercial consumer products?
options: A label listing the names and phone numbers of company executives
A voluntary or mandatory certification label informing consumers that a product meets verified environmental standards across its life cycle
A barcode scanned by supermarket cashiers at the checkout counter
A price tag showing how much money an item costs in cash
10.explanation: Standardized ecolabels (e.g. EU Ecolabel, Energy Star, FSC) empower conscious consumers to differentiate genuinely sustainable products.

10.question: What is 'Energy Star' certification on domestic electrical appliances?
options: A sticker showing that an appliance was made in a movie studio
A guarantee that an appliance will never need to be cleaned
An international standard indicating that an appliance meets strict government energy efficiency guidelines, consuming less power than standard models
A label indicating that an appliance operates using nuclear rocket fuel
10.explanation: Energy Star certified appliances (refrigerators, washers, monitors) consume 10–50% less electricity, slashing household utility bills and grid emissions.

10.question: What is a 'deposit-return scheme' (DRS) for beverage containers?
options: A system where consumers pay a small deposit when buying a canned/bottled drink, which is refunded when they return the empty container for recycling
A prize awarded to the person who drinks the most soda in one hour
A fine charged to people who drink water in public parks
A bank account where citizens deposit coins to earn interest
10.explanation: Reverse vending machines and deposit refunds achieve recovery rates exceeding 90% for PET bottles and aluminium cans, eliminating roadside litter.

10.question: What is 'single-use plastic' and why are many nations banning it?
options: Disposable plastics (straws, bags, cutlery) used only once before being discarded, which persist in the environment for centuries and pollute oceans
Plastic steering wheels installed inside commercial automobiles
Durable plastic pipes used to supply drinking water to cities for fifty years
Plastic glasses worn by people to improve their eyesight
10.explanation: Single-use items fragment into persistent microplastics, choking wildlife and overwhelming municipal waste collection systems.

10.question: What are 'bioplastics' manufactured from plant biomass (e.g. PLA from corn starch)?
options: Plastics extracted from wild ocean coral reef colonies
Plastics that dissolve into pure gasoline when placed in water
Plastics derived from renewable biological resources rather than petroleum crude oil, some of which are commercially compostable under heat
Plastics made from radioactive uranium ores in nuclear laboratories
10.explanation: Polylactic acid (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) replace fossil hydrocarbons, though industrial composting facilities are needed for degradation.

10.question: What is an environmental limitation of many commercially marketed 'biodegradable' plastics?
options: They freeze surrounding river water into solid ice blocks
They turn into solid steel metal when placed in soil
They emit toxic radioactive rays when exposed to sunlight
They require high temperatures and specific humidity in industrial composting facilities to break down, and will not degrade quickly in the cold ocean
10.explanation: Consumers mistakenly litter 'biodegradable' plastics in marine waters, where lack of thermophilic heat prevents breakdown, mimicking normal plastics.

10.question: What is 'industrial symbiosis' (eco-industrial parks)?
options: Two companies competing against each other to sell identical products
A group of factory workers playing music together during lunch breaks
An industrial zone where all factories produce the exact same item
An industrial ecosystem where waste, by-products, or rejected energy of one industrial company are utilized as raw materials or energy by another nearby company
10.explanation: Exemplified by Kalundborg in Denmark, waste steam, fly ash, sludge, and sulfur circulate across oil refineries, power stations, and farms.

10.question: What is the 'Polluter Pays Principle' in environmental jurisprudence?
options: A policy that makes it illegal to fine corporate factory owners
The legal principle that those who produce pollution should bear the full financial costs of managing, cleaning up, and remedying the environmental damage
A system where polluters receive cash awards from national governments
A law ordering taxpayers to pay all fines incurred by private factories
10.explanation: Polluter-pays internalizes negative environmental externalities into corporate balance sheets, discouraging reckless industrial disposal.

10.question: What is the 'Precautionary Principle' in environmental policymaking?
options: The principle that if an action or policy has a suspected risk of causing severe harm to the public or environment, lack of full scientific certainty shall not delay cost-effective preventive action
A rule stating that no action should ever be taken to protect the environment
A requirement that all scientific research must be approved by military generals
An instruction to wait until thousands of people die before investigating a chemical
10.explanation: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration establishes that preventive action must anticipate irreversible ecological harm even amidst scientific uncertainty.

10.question: What is the 'Convention on Biological Diversity' (CBD)?
options: A commercial treaty governing the export of timber logs between countries
A law ordering all farmers to grow only one variety of corn worldwide
A multilateral treaty dedicated to the conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources
An international agreement to build zoos in every major city in the world
10.explanation: Signed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, the CBD establishes global biodiversity frameworks, national action plans (NBSAPs), and genetic access protocols.

10.question: What landmark target was agreed at the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (COP15)?
options: A target to cut down 30% of all global forests by the year 2030
The '30 by 30' target: protecting and conserving at least 30% of Earth's land, inland waters, and coastal and marine areas by 2030
An agreement to ban the ownership of domestic pets by the year 2030
A plan to build 30 new coal power stations in every country worldwide
10.explanation: The 30x30 target mobilizes international funding to halt species extinction and double globally protected ecological reserves.

10.question: What is the 'Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants' (POPs)?
options: A private club for European organic vegetable farmers
An agreement to share agricultural tractor machinery between nations
A treaty governing international commercial airline flight routes
An international environmental treaty aimed at eliminating or restricting the production and use of toxic, bioaccumulative, persistent chemicals ('the dirty dozen')
10.explanation: The Stockholm Convention phases out dangerous organochlorine pesticides (DDT, chlordane), PCBs, and unintentionally produced dioxins.

10.question: Why are 'Persistent Organic Pollutants' (POPs) uniquely dangerous globally?
options: They resist chemical and biological degradation, bioaccumulate in fatty tissues of living organisms, and travel long distances via atmospheric wind currents to polar zones
They dissolve completely in rainwater within five seconds of being sprayed
They turn into solid gold crystals when exposed to cold winter frost
They make plants grow ten times taller without requiring any sunlight
10.explanation: The 'grasshopper effect' transports volatile lipophilic POPs to cold polar latitudes, where they magnify in marine mammals and indigenous breast milk.

10.question: What is the 'Kyoto Protocol' (adopted in 1997)?
options: An international agreement to build nuclear power plants across the Sahara
The first international agreement under the UNFCCC committing industrialized countries to legally binding greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets
A law ordering all commercial ships to sail with empty fuel tanks
A treaty requiring countries to ban the use of bicycles in major cities
10.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol introduced binding reduction caps for Annex I developed states alongside market mechanisms (CDM, Joint Implementation).

10.question: What was the 'Clean Development Mechanism' (CDM) under the Kyoto Protocol?
options: A military program that built weapons testing facilities in desert areas
An agreement that forced developing countries to close all their factories
A mechanism allowing industrialized nations with emission limits to invest in emission-reduction projects in developing nations to earn tradable carbon credits
A program that built luxury tourist hotels in tropical beach resorts
10.explanation: The CDM channeled private capital into renewable energy and methane capture projects in the Global South, generating certified emission reductions (CERs).

10.question: What is 'ecological footprint'?
options: The physical shoe size of an environmental scientist working in a park
The length of a hiking trail running through a mountain valley
The area of land covered by dead leaves in an autumn forest
A metric measuring how much biologically productive land and sea area an individual, population, or activity requires to produce the resources it consumes and absorb its wastes
10.explanation: Expressed in global hectares (gha), ecological footprint analysis evaluates whether human resource demands exceed planetary biocapacity.

10.question: What is 'Earth Overshoot Day'?
options: The day when all satellites in space complete one full orbit around Earth
The calendar date on which humanity's resource consumption for the year exceeds Earth's capacity to regenerate those resources in that year
A global public holiday celebrating the arrival of spring flowers

10.question: What is 'green building' (sustainable architecture)?
options: Building homes using only synthetic plastic toy bricks
Painting all exterior walls and windows of a building with green paint
Designing, constructing, and operating buildings to reduce or eliminate negative environmental impacts through energy efficiency, renewable energy, and sustainable materials
Constructing skyscrapers without any windows or doors
10.explanation: Standards like LEED and BREEAM evaluate solar orientation, rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling, low-VOC materials, and net-zero energy.

10.question: What is a 'living roof' (green roof)?
options: A roof made of bare corrugated iron sheets painted bright yellow
A building roof partially or completely covered with vegetation and a growing medium, providing building insulation, stormwater retention, and urban wildlife habitat
A roof covered with thick black petroleum asphalt tar
A roof constructed from transparent glass windows that cannot open
10.explanation: Vegetated green roofs absorb 70–90% of stormwater runoff, attenuate urban heat islands, and cut HVAC heating and cooling loads by 25%.

10.question: What is 'circular fashion' in textile and consumer resource management?
options: Manufacturing clothes using disposable paper toilet tissue
Designing and producing clothing to be durable, repairable, reusable, and recyclable, keeping textile fibres circulating in closed loops without landfill disposal
Throwing shirts into the garbage after wearing them for one day
Weaving clothing in circular circular ring shapes only
10.explanation: Circular fashion eliminates virgin fossil synthetic inputs, scaling up mechanical/chemical fibre recycling, garment leasing, and organic fabrics.

10.question: What is 'community composting'?
options: Setting fire to garden leaves on residential sidewalks on weekends
Dumping household trash bags in public street intersections at night
A neighborhood or municipal system where local residents pool kitchen food scraps and yard trimmings to create organic compost for local community gardens
Flushing vegetable peels down residential bathroom toilets
10.explanation: Decentralized community compost bins divert organic matter from landfills, slashing methane emissions and regenerating urban soil tilth.

10.question: What does 'Think Globally, Act Locally' mean in environmental management?
options: Traveling around the world on airplanes every weekend to clean beaches
Buying only imported foreign goods to avoid supporting local farmers
Forbidding citizens from knowing what happens in foreign countries
Understanding that global environmental challenges (like climate change and biodiversity loss) require collective individual and community actions in everyday life
10.explanation: Global planetary ecological crises are mitigated through cumulative decentralized local choices: recycling, energy conservation, and local stewardship.
